📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that overview The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization. The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access. Threat The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards. Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors: Authentication bypass; Arbitrary code injection; and Weak configurations. Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects: Change of temperature, which could: Affect the service life of the system; Create a fire hazard; Cause loss of inventory; or Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage. Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition). Mitigations The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement: Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices. Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I]. Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F]. Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance. Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H]. Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O]. Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity. For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets. Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations. Resources The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations: CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT Contact Information The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet: Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office. When available, please include the following information regarding the incident: Date, time, and location of the incident; Type of activity; Number of people affected; Type of equipment used for the activity; and Name of the submitting organization or organization, and a designated point of contact. Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA has added one upcoming vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-19868 SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Use of Single-factor Authentication Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not presently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

CISA has added one newly introduced vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

It has been revealed that while BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Recent findings suggest that if your manufacturer already runs on Google Cloud, adding a fresh vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:.

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

It has been revealed that every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

In a recent development, once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

According to recent reports, your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

#5156. How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2003 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group.
  • Proving, one use case at a time, that AI systems follow it is another.
  • Recent findings suggest that standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group.

Having an AI policy is one thing. Proving, one use case at a time, that AI systems follow it is another. Every upcoming generative AI application adds one more system to prove. Teams can now build one in days, but each still needs a risk committee’s approval before it reaches customers or employees. When that approval depends on reviewers reading documents and testing the system by hand, governance becomes the slowest step in the pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof. Working with AWS Professional Services, the bank deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard that show what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. This post explains how the assessment runs on AWS and what Standard Bank Group learned from its first runs.

Standard Bank Group didn’t need a newly introduced AI policy. Like most large banks, it already had an established model risk practice that covers concerns such as explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case according to its level of risk before it goes live.

Generative AI increases the complexity, because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case still needs to meet the same high security and compliance bar.

“At Standard Bank, this assessment demonstrates how we are working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into our AI journey, allowing us to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. We believe responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence.”.

— Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer, Standard Bank Group.

According to recent reports, the goal was to automate evidence gathering and testing, then feed the results into the approval gates Standard Bank Group already runs. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, but the committee now bases each decision on consistent evidence, collected the same way across use cases.

Figure 1 reveals how the assessment’s components fit together in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting.

Figure 1: The assessment pipeline in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting.

The assessment runs entirely in Standard Bank Group’s own AWS account. Documents, code, and test results stay in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket there. The AWS Well-Architected Tool handles intake, AWS Step Functions orchestrates the pipeline, and a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock evaluates the evidence. It uses a technique called LLM-as-a-judge, in which a large language model checks evidence against defined criteria.

With Amazon Bedrock, Standard Bank Group could use a foundation model without stepping outside the controls it already runs on AWS. The bank controls access to the model through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), just as it does for its other AWS workloads. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t share the bank’s prompts or model outputs with model providers, and doesn’t use them to train models. Because Amazon Bedrock offers many foundation models through one API, the team can move to a newer judge model by changing a configuration setting instead of rebuilding the pipeline.

It has been revealed that each assessment moves through four steps. In the first two, a pre-assessment agent collects evidence about the use case, then the pipeline examines it and tests the application directly. The third evaluates that evidence against controls. The fourth summarizes the results in a standard, predefined format and delivers them to the people who act on them.

The custom lens in the Well-Architected Tool holds about 40 questions, each covering a risk event such as incomplete technical documentation or insufficient human oversight. Delivery teams no longer fill it in from scratch. A pre-assessment agent running on AWS Fargate scans the use case’s code repository and documentation. It maps relevant files to each question and pre-populates the lens with answers and links to the evidence. The delivery team then reviews those answers, corrects any mistakes, and adds the evidence the agent couldn’t find.

The pipeline works from four kinds of evidence.

According to recent reports, for documents and code, the pipeline checks whether each artifact contains what its mapped control requires. Each control comes from an international AI standard or framework, or from Standard Bank Group’s own policies. An incident procedure, for example, needs to describe how incidents are reported.

For live testing, the pipeline calls the application through its AWS Lambda function or API. The delivery team supplies questions a typical user would ask. The pipeline adds a built-in set of jailbreak attempts and off-topic questions, which the application is expected to decline. It also sends the same prompt several times, in its original and reworded forms, and uses an embedding model on Amazon Bedrock to check that the answers stay consistent in meaning. Where the team provides expected answers, the pipeline measures how closely the responses match them. Every response is stored in Amazon S3, so reviewers can see exactly what the application generated.

In this step, a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock acts as the judge. The assessment uses the model as-is with no fine-tuning or customization. (Model availability varies by AWS Region, so check the supported models by Region before you deploy.) For each question, the model checks whether specific evidence appears in the artifacts and in the application’s responses, and returns yes or no.

Every check maps to a control in an international standard or framework for AI management, AI risk, or AI security. Standard Bank Group also customized the lens with judge questions built from its own standards, bringing the total to more than 300. The checks cover the eight AWS responsible AI dimensions in the following table:.

Industry observers note that each risk receives a likelihood score, the share of required evidence the model couldn’t find, and a fixed severity level that the bank’s risk team can adjust. Together they produce a rating from Very low to Critical. Each missing piece of evidence maps to a specific mitigation and to the clause of the standard or policy it came from. A risk officer can then trace any findings back to their source when explaining decisions to a regulator. Figure 2 follows one missing piece of evidence through this process, from the evidence request to the recommended fix.

Figure 2: How one finding is traced from evidence to fix.

Standard Bank Group protects and checks the assessment’s output in two ways. Every AI model interaction is protected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, ensuring alignment with the bank’s established security and responsible AI standards. The assessment’s model calls pass through the same safeguards the bank enforces across its AWS accounts for its AI workloads. These guardrails screen for harmful content and for attempts to manipulate the model.

The assessment is also designed so its output can be checked. Instead of asking the model for an open-ended opinion, the pipeline asks narrow yes-or-no questions, each worded to match a specific control. A fixed formula that the risk team can inspect turns those answers into scores. Each evaluation runs multiple times to measure how consistent the answers are and any inconsistent findings are flagged in the review interface. Every judgment is stored with the evidence behind it so that reviewers and auditors can trace how it was reached.

It has been revealed that the pipeline summarizes the results in a standard format and delivers them as an executive presentation, a mitigation checklist, a detailed technical report, and an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that tracks scores across use cases over time. Before a gate decision, reviewers confirm findings in a custom review interface with single sign-on. There they can add the use case, review the questions, amend answers with a business justification, and rewrite the output.

The assessment produces evidence against controls. It doesn’t certify compliance with any regulation, and Standard Bank Group remains responsible for its own regulatory determinations.

International standards give every use case a common baseline, but the bank’s risk committees approve use cases against its own policy. A question factory addresses this by generating extra judge questions from internal documents. Standard Bank Group’s risk team used it to turn internal policies into checks that run on every use case.

Because those checks are derived directly from policy language, a policy change becomes a test change. Every subsequent assessment applies the updated rule automatically, with minimal manual rework by the risk team.

In a recent development, “Most organizations treat policy as something you read. Standard Bank Group treats it as something you run. When every rule becomes a check that runs against the live system, a policy update stops being a memo and becomes a test. That fundamentally changes how fast a bank can scale AI responsibly.”.

— Sri Elaprolu, Director, Frontier AI Science & Engineering, AWS.

Industry observers note that the assessment fits into three stages of the use case lifecycle. During a proof of concept, it is optional, giving teams an early view of potential gaps. At the build stage, it becomes mandatory, and the approval gate draws on its results as formal evidence. Today the assessment runs in Standard Bank Group’s production environment, evaluating use cases before they go live. After live workloads are connected, the assessment will rerun on a schedule or whenever code or configuration changes, keeping the evidence current well beyond launch. The bank’s teams already trigger assessments on their own through a central system where use cases flow from intake to evaluation in a single workflow.

At Standard Bank Group, the assessment reduced a traditionally manual two-week review to a comprehensive risk report generated in approximately two hours, demonstrated across six assessments. It also delivered a 14% improvement in use-case risk scores after remediation. This strengthens responsible AI governance, reduces compliance bottlenecks, and shortens the path from assessment to production.

This approach can benefit three groups involved in approving AI use cases:.

According to recent reports, “Adoption of AI at scale across the enterprise requires trust, both internally and with our customers. This assessment is proving key in enabling all our product teams to demonstrate that they are building enterprise-grade solutions aligned with both our own and industry best practices.”.

— Duncan Macdonald, Chief Technology Officer, Standard Bank Group.

Banks designed approval gates for systems that changed a few times a year. Generative AI applications change with every prompt upgrade, model version, and new data source. As they take on more autonomous tasks, the number of decisions that need evidence keeps growing. Adding reviewers can’t keep pace with that rate of change.

Standard Bank Group’s approach points to a different operating model. When policies become tests and evidence is collected automatically, governance moves out of a checkpoint at the end of delivery and into the system itself. Every AI application in the portfolio can carry a current, auditable record of how it meets the bank’s standards, refreshed whenever its code or configuration changes. Risk teams spend their time on judgment calls and policy design, and the bank can show regulators the same evidence it uses for its own decisions.

According to recent reports, the same foundation extends further. Continuous reassessment keeps evidence aligned with a changing code base after launch. New regulations can be encoded once as checks and applied across every use case. Aggregated scores give boards an enterprise-wide view of AI risk instead of a collection of individual reviews.

For any institution scaling AI, the question worth asking is how many of its policies have ever been tested against a running system. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA has added six fresh vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference Vulnerability  CVE-2026-111560 Barracuda Networks Multiple Products OS Command Injection Vulnerability  CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres Vulnerability  CVE-2026-116606 Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG) Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability  CVE-2026-124194 Microsoft Office Outlook Missing User Interaction for Potentially Unsafe Action Vulnerability  CVE-2026-125350 Google Chromium Use-After-Free Vulnerability  These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not at the moment listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document.
  • Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors.
  • Industry observers note that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

Industry observers note that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

In a recent development, this post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

It has been revealed that pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

Industry observers note that A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:.

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d.

Recent findings suggest that even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

Sources indicate that the useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:.

According to recent reports, with pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:.

Recent findings suggest that this distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

It has been revealed that adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Sources indicate that rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:.

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

In a recent development, pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

It has been revealed that if you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:.

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​.

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives upgrade the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:.

According to recent reports, cachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

Recent findings suggest that multiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

Industry observers note that the poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:.

The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:.

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:.

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

According to recent reports, sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:.

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:.

Sources indicate that both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

Sources indicate that for adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

Industry observers note that the gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:.

Industry observers note that if the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

Industry observers note that multiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

#5145. Industry News: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: One endpoint across Regions and clusters

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1400 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: One endpoint across Regions and clusters

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1400 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During a traffic peak, a request can sit in a queue on a saturated HyperPod cluster while GPUs on another cluster, sometimes in another AWS Region, sit idle.
  • It has been revealed that in Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway, we demonstrated how the Inference Gateway gives each Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster a single, GPU-aware endpoint.
  • Sources indicate that today, SageMaker HyperPod introduces the Global Inference Gateway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During a traffic peak, a request can sit in a queue on a saturated HyperPod cluster while GPUs on another cluster, sometimes in another AWS Region, sit idle. You have already paid for that capacity, but your requests can’t reach it.

It has been revealed that in Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway, we demonstrated how the Inference Gateway gives each Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster a single, GPU-aware endpoint. It reads real-time signals such as key-value (KV) cache utilization and queue depth to place every request on the best-suited pod. That solves routing inside one cluster, but not across clusters.

Sources indicate that today, SageMaker HyperPod introduces the Global Inference Gateway. It is one SageMaker-managed gateway that routes across every cluster you register, in one Region or across Regions. The gateway picks the cluster and carries the request over the AWS backbone, with automatic failover and authentication through AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Inside each cluster, the Inference Gateway keeps picking the pod, unchanged. The Global Inference Gateway is the second tier of the architecture we described in part 1.

Models are getting larger, and the GPU capacity to serve them is harder to find. To get enough of it, you spread it across more clusters and more Regions.

Consider a team that serves four models across five HyperPod clusters in two Regions. Without the Inference Gateway, clients track 20 endpoints: one per model per cluster. The Inference Gateway cuts that to five, one per cluster. But each client still picks a cluster itself.

The team needs one endpoint that sends each request to the best-suited cluster and moves traffic off a failed cluster on its own.

The Global Inference Gateway helps you get more from the GPU capacity you already have, with less to operate.

Industry observers note that “At Bagelcode, we run our own LLM inference service on AWS to help teams across the company, including our game teams, use AI to improve how they work. In our beta tests, the Global Inference Gateway in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod routed requests across two AWS Regions through a single endpoint and kept serving them when one cluster could no longer serve the model. That gave our small platform team cross-Region failover without having to build or maintain our own routing layer.”.

— Jinhyung Park, VP (AI Platform), Bagelcode.

Setting up the gateway takes two decisions: which clusters to open up for routing, and which of them to group behind one gateway.

A cluster is reachable only after you publish it. When you publish a cluster, the controller creates a Network Load Balancer in front of the cluster’s Inference Gateway, publishes a virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint service on it, and uploads the listener’s certificate to your TLS bucket. These resources live in your account. If you list a cluster in a gateway before you publish it, the call fails with a message that tells you what to fix.

Figure 1 shows the path of each request: (1) your client signs the request with SigV4 and sends it to the gateway’s regional endpoint. (2) The gateway authenticates the caller and picks the best cluster. (3) AWS PrivateLink carries the request to that cluster, in the same Region or another, and (4) the cluster’s Inference Gateway routes it to a model pod, as it does today.

Figure 1: The Global Inference Gateway receives each request at one regional endpoint and forwards it over AWS PrivateLink to the best HyperPod cluster, where the cluster’s Inference Gateway routes it to a model pod. Each cluster publishes its load back to the gateway.

In a recent development, you decide which clusters to publish, which to group behind a gateway, and how to weight routing. AWS operates the rest:.

On each cluster, a service-managed metrics publisher with its own IAM role sends the cluster’s load to the gateway.

In a recent development, for each request, the gateway scores every healthy cluster on four signals and sends the request to the highest-scoring cluster. Each cluster’s metrics publisher supplies the load signals.

Recent findings suggest that you control how much each signal counts with routing weights. Each weight is a value from 0.0 to 1.0, and a weight of 0 turns that signal off. If you set weights, you set all four, and they must add up to 1.0. If you omit them, the defaults in the following table apply.

It has been revealed that the defaults favor clusters close to the gateway’s Region, while still moving traffic toward clusters with available capacity and away from clusters that are failing. If resilience matters more than proximity for your workload, raise ErrorRate and lower RegionProximity. For example, the following routing block weights recent errors at 0.7:.

You pass the weights in the Routing parameter of CreateGlobalInferenceGateway, and you can change them later with UpdateGlobalInferenceGateway.

Your path depends on what you run today. If you serve from a single cluster, stay on that cluster’s Inference Gateway endpoint. Move to the Global Inference Gateway when you add a second cluster.

Recent findings suggest that to set up the Global Inference Gateway, you prepare each cluster, create an execution role, and call CreateGlobalInferenceGateway. You then send OpenAI-compatible requests, signed with SigV4, to the gateway endpoint. For step-by-step instructions, including the IAM roles and policies, see the AWS documentation.

Every request to the gateway is signed with SigV4 and authorized with IAM. Callers need permission to invoke the gateway, and streaming has its own action:.

Sources indicate that attach this policy to each IAM identity that sends requests. To allow every gateway in the account, use global-inference-gateway/* as the resource.

Recent findings suggest that the execution role follows least privilege. It can describe only the clusters you list, reach only their Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) API, and read only the routing certificates under the gig/ prefix of your TLS bucket, tagged as created by HyperPod Inference.

In a recent development, identity tokens. If your clusters check JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), pass the token with --customer-identity-token (the X-Amzn-SageMaker-Customer-Identity-Token header), with no Bearer prefix. The token travels inside the SigV4 signature, so an unsigned token is rejected with 403 and a repeated token with 400. Turn on JWT checks on every cluster that serves a model, or on none of them, so a request doesn’t succeed on one cluster and fail on another.

Requests reach your clusters only through AWS PrivateLink, as shown in Figure 1. The gateway does not log or store prompts or completions.

Here are steps to configure the gateway.

Prepare the latest cluster and create the execution role’s EKS access entry on it, as described in the documentation. Also add the new cluster to the Resource lists of the execution role’s permissions policy. Then call AddInferenceGateway in the gateway’s Region, even if the new cluster is in another Region:.

The gateway validates the cluster and starts routing to it once it is healthy. The endpoint, other clusters, and clients aren’t affected.

Call RemoveInferenceGateway in the gateway’s Region:.

Recent findings suggest that the gateway stops sending new requests to the cluster, lets in-flight requests finish, and removes the private endpoint. A gateway always keeps at least one cluster. To withdraw the cluster fully, set globalRouting.enabled: false in its InferenceGatewayConfig and reapply it.

Call DeleteGlobalInferenceGateway:.

Recent findings suggest that the gateway endpoint stops serving, and per-cluster endpoints keep serving. After the gateway is deleted, withdraw each cluster with globalRouting.enabled: false, then delete the execution role and the IAM permissions you added for global routing.

The following table summarizes how common events and changes affect traffic.

For any troubleshooting assistance, please see the Troubleshooting Guide.

In a recent development, in this post, we introduced the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: one SageMaker-managed endpoint across your HyperPod clusters, in one Region or several. The gateway picks the cluster based on KV cache headroom, queue depth, Region proximity, and error rate, and moves traffic off a failed cluster with no client changes.

According to recent reports, the Global Inference Gateway is available in 13 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Singapore), and Asia Pacific (Sydney).

To get started, see the AWS documentation.

#5140. BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time.
  • Sources indicate that tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment.
  • In a recent development, building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.

Sources indicate that tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4).

In a recent development, building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps people entirely in control of their digital lives.

BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

Learning from demonstrations (SFT).

We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Industry observers note that next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages).

In a recent development, finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

In a recent development, each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Recent findings suggest that table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Recent findings suggest that tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

Recent findings suggest that table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

In a recent development, the largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

It has been revealed that botPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

It has been revealed that on complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

According to recent reports, shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

According to recent reports, fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):.

It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

According to recent reports, botPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

[1] Yu, Qiying, et al. "DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025): 113222–113244.

[2] Zhang, Shaokun, et al. "Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning." International Conference on Learning Representations (2026).

[3] Qian, Cheng, et al. "ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025).

General Recommendations Operators of critical power systems (e.g. TSOs or DSOs) worldwide are usually required by regulations to build resilience into the power grids by applying multi-level redundant secondary protection schemes. It is therefore recommended that the operators check whether appropriate resilient protection measures are in place. The risk of cyber incidents impacting the grid's reliability can thus be minimized by virtue of the grid design. Siemens strongly recommends applying the provided security updates using the corresponding tooling and documented procedures made available with the product. If supported by the product, an automated means to apply the security updates across multiple product instances may be used. Siemens strongly recommends prior validation of any security update before being applied, and supervision by trained staff of the update process in the target environment. As a general security measure Siemens strongly recommends protecting network access with appropriate mechanisms (e.g. firewalls, segmentation, VPN). It is advised to configure the environment according to our operational guidelines in order to run the devices in a protected IT environment. Recommended security guidelines can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/gridsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends people take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. #5134. The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2533 w)
