The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs.
  • 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment.
  • TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

The same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

Industry observers note that our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are key for our task.

Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

According to recent reports, loRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

Recent findings suggest that hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:.

Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

Industry observers note that the sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

It has been revealed that O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

In a recent development, in the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

Industry observers note that A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:.

Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:.

We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:.

Recent findings suggest that this container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

In a recent development, we use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

If you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

In a recent development, the commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:.

Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso.

We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

According to recent reports, we also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object.

Industry observers note that the first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

Sources indicate that we keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

Sources indicate that it’s vital to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

Sources indicate that the snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

We then follow these steps within the training loop:.

According to recent reports, the training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

It has been revealed that for each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

Sources indicate that we trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

In a recent development, the training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls promptly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

Industry observers note that the figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:.

Sources indicate that in the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

Sources indicate that phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

Gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

Thank you for following along, and see you in the next one! 👋🤗.

Sources indicate that CISA has added one newly introduced vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-115731 Perforce Puppet Enterprise Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not right now listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Breaking: Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (192 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.24845v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.

#5128. Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3531 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Keeping a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development in sync entails keeping several separately maintained pieces of configuration matched to what’s running on the nodes.
  • We believe cluster configurations should be managed the way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure.
  • In this post, we walk through the features we introduced in 2026 and explain why the software on running nodes needed a different mechanism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Keeping a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development in sync entails keeping several separately maintained pieces of configuration matched to what’s running on the nodes. The cluster’s shape lives on multiple configuration files, its software in custom scripts, its network topology in files that must be edited as nodes change, and its users in a roster that an administrator must maintain and rerun. Over time these pieces drift away from what’s actually running, and nothing tells you when they do.

We believe cluster configurations should be managed the way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. You declare what you want through an API or the console, AWS validates it before it’s applied, the cluster is kept in that state continuously, and you can see whether it’s working. During 2026, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod brought that approach to Slurm clusters, with API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based configuration, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management, and deep health checks. Today, we rolled out cluster extensions, which bring the same approach to the software and settings on running nodes, with managed extensions for observability and user management. However, through all of it, you still keep full access to every node in your cluster, including the controller node. You can SSH in, configure nodes directly, and run your own lifecycle scripts. The APIs give you less to maintain, direct access gives you more control, and you choose the balance.

In this post, we walk through the features we introduced in 2026 and explain why the software on running nodes needed a different mechanism. We then show how cluster extensions work, through both the API and the console, and follow a platform team through a quarter on a cluster that uses them.

Industry observers note that we can think of a Slurm cluster’s configuration grouped into six layers. Five of them describe the cluster itself: its definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health. The sixth covers the software running on its nodes, which we discuss in the next section. The following figure shows the six layers.

According to recent reports, earlier in 2026, we brought declarative management to the first five layers. With API-driven Slurm configuration, administrators define node roles, partitions, and Amazon FSx for Lustre and Amazon FSx for OpenZFS mounts in CreateCluster and UpdateCluster requests, and connect an external accounting database. HyperPod updates partition settings while preserving other controller-node Slurm customizations. AMI-based configuration replaces routine setup scripts with images preconfigured with Slurm, Docker, Enroot, Pyxis, and home directories. A custom AMI or OnInitComplete script handles organization-specific software. Continuous provisioning for Slurm retries capacity requests in the background; AMI-based configuration works with it, minimum capacity requirements let teams specify MinInstanceCount, and cluster operations track scaling requests.

According to recent reports, automatic topology management maintains the network layout as nodes scale or are replaced. On Slurm 25.11 or later, partition-level topology supports tree or block topology per partition. For hardware health, on-demand deep health checks stress GPUs and test NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) connectivity, while deep health checks with continuous provisioning run as nodes are provisioned. Nodes under check stay in Slurm maintenance reservations until checks finish, keeping jobs off them.

According to recent reports, the five layers described so far are configurations that HyperPod can derive or apply once, when it provisions a node. The sixth layer, the software that runs on the nodes, behaves differently because it keeps changing for the life of the cluster. As researchers join and leave, a team asks for deeper GPU metrics for a week, and an exporter ships a fix. For this layer, lifecycle scripts have been the main mechanism so far, and they have drawbacks when the software keeps changing. A script runs only when a node is provisioned, so each change means editing it and then replacing nodes or rerunning it across the fleet. A mistake reveals only when the script runs on a node, and nothing reports what’s installed, so nodes drift apart over time.

We wanted the software to be declared in one place, checked when you submit it, kept consistent across nodes, and visible afterward. In November 2026, we launched cluster extensions, which are software packages managed by AWS that you install, configure, update, and remove through APIs or the Amazon SageMaker AI console, starting with observability and user management, including directory integration, as the first software extensions. Compared with scripts, extensions have these advantages:.

Use cluster extensions when HyperPod offers a managed software capability. Use custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts for organization-specific software or initialization that the available extensions don’t cover. HyperPod supports two cluster managed extensions today:.

The following diagram demonstrates how an extension reaches your nodes.

Figure 2: HyperPod can install, edit, or remove an extension. HyperPod records the desired configuration, a node agent applies the extension package on every node, including fresh and replaced ones, and health probes report status and health concerns back.

You can use cluster extensions from the SageMaker AI console or through an API. On the console, the Extensions tab on a cluster’s details page lists each extension with its status, version, and ARN, and it’s where you install a upcoming one. Each extension adds controls of its own, such as the metric store and an open dashboard in Grafana button for observability, and the number of users and groups and a Manage users button for user management. You can also manage every extension through APIs, from the AWS CLI or an SDK, to script installs, keep settings in version control, repeat a setup across clusters, or check status and health from your own tooling. The following table lists the six cluster extension APIs, from installing an extension to listing the versions you can upgrade to, along with console view for extensions.

Figure 3: Left, the six cluster extension APIs and what each one does. Right, the console view to add and remove extensions.

The following diagram shows what happens after you call one of these APIs.

Figure 4: You declare an extension’s version and settings through the API. HyperPod validates and records them, applies them to every node for its role, and reports status and health.

Recent findings suggest that when you create or enhancement an extension, HyperPod validates your settings against the version’s schema during the API call, so a misspelled setting is rejected immediately. It then records the version and settings as the desired state and applies them, with each node installing only what its role needs, such as GPU exporters on GPU nodes only. Newly introduced and replacement nodes get the same state a few minutes after they start, and every node reports whether the extension applied and whether it’s healthy.

Sources indicate that updates send only the settings that you want to change, and HyperPod merges them into the stored settings. Problems that show up only on a node, such as a port or user ID that something else already uses, appear in the Health field of DescribeClusterExtension, grouped by cause with a code, a message, and a count of affected nodes. HyperPod retries internal failures on its own, and for anything else you fix the cause and call UpdateClusterExtension with no changes to retry the affected nodes.

Industry observers note that an extension’s status is Creating or Updating while a change rolls out, Active when every node runs the requested version and settings and none reports a problem, and Degraded when some nodes failed or report a problem. Each extension has its own ARN, so a platform team can own sagemaker-user-management while a monitoring team owns sagemaker-observability. Each health glitch names the component, describes the effect on your cluster, gives the next step, and counts the affected nodes, so you can see where to look without signing in to each node, as the following figure shows.

Figure 5: An extension’s status, and an example health issue for a node exporter that isn’t running.

In a recent development, A useful way to decide is to ask who owns the software and how often it changes. Some of the software on a cluster is specific to your organization, such as security agents, license servers, and the storage layout your data pipeline expects. Lifecycle scripts and custom AMIs are the right tools for it, because only your team knows what it needs. The rest is software that almost every cluster needs, like GPU and job metrics and user accounts with consistent IDs and access rules. That software must match on every node and keeps changing, so cluster extensions are the better fit, because you declare it once, HyperPod validates it, and each extension reports whether it’s healthy.

In a recent development, the two approaches can coexist, but each component should have one owner. Don’t manage the same exporter, user, or service through both a lifecycle script and an extension, because competing configurations can cause installation or runtime conflicts. Cluster extensions work with every lifecycle configuration option.

Recent findings suggest that if you already run these capabilities from scripts, you can move to extensions one capability at a time, and scripts and extensions can run side by side while you do. For each capability, the migration takes four steps:.

Recent findings suggest that if anything is left behind, the install names the conflict, such as a port that’s already in use, and DescribeClusterExtension shows it under Health. With user management, you keep the same usernames and user IDs. The following figure shows four steps.

Figure 6: Moving an existing cluster from lifecycle scripts to extensions, one capability at a time.

You need a HyperPod Slurm cluster on or after the November 2, 2026 HyperPod AMI or later with continuous provisioning enabled. An extension runs software as root on every node, so treat CreateClusterExtension, UpdateClusterExtension, and DeleteClusterExtension as administrator permissions. We suggest that you do not grant them to the cluster’s execution role, because every user who can sign in to the nodes can use its credentials. That role does need access to the destinations that the extensions use, which means Amazon CloudWatch or aps:RemoteWrite for observability and secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the Active Directory secrets that user management reads. If those secrets are encrypted with a customer managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key, the role also needs kms:Decrypt on that key. User management also needs a shared file system, such as Amazon FSx for Lustre, for home directories.

For procedures, IAM policies, and configuration references, see Cluster extensions for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm clusters in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide.

To see how cluster extensions are used in practice, consider a platform team that manages a shared Slurm cluster for several research groups. The team needs a reviewable cluster definition, GPU and job metrics, corporate directory access, local accounts for a partner lab, and separate ownership of observability and user management. The following examples show how the team configures these capabilities and responds to routine changes and failures.

The administrator declares the whole cluster, including node roles, partitions, FSx mounts, minimum capacity, deep health checks, and the external accounting database, in a single CreateCluster request. For a complete example request, see Getting started with SageMaker HyperPod using the AWS CLI.

The request has no lifecycle configuration, topology file, or Slurm configuration file. Each SlurmConfig gives its instance group a role, and the GPU group joins the train partition. AMI-based configuration sets up the nodes, and the security team’s compliance agent is already in the custom AMI. The GPU group asks for 8 nodes and requires 6, so jobs can start as soon as 6 are ready while HyperPod provisions the rest and health checks each GPU node as it arrives. HyperPod selects tree topology for the P5 nodes on its own, and accounting writes to an Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) database that the team owns. The administrator can still SSH into the controller node to inspect or tune Slurm directly.

It has been revealed that leadership wants GPU and job metrics, so the administrator installs the observability extension. In the SageMaker AI console, on the cluster’s Extensions tab, the administrator chooses the observability extension, picks the metric categories and their levels and the collection interval, and selects one of two metric stores: Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus. The following screenshot shows the install form with one store selected. The other option is available in the same field.

Figure 7: Installing the observability extension from the console, with configurable metric levels and a choice of metric store.

The same installation through the API takes one create-cluster-extension call. The following example uses Amazon CloudWatch as the metric store. To send metrics to Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus instead, you set the Prometheus destination in the same configuration.

The administrator installs the extension with one create-cluster-extension call:.

The call returns the extension’s ARN, which the administrator uses in later calls:.

In a recent development, whichever way it’s installed, each node runs only the components relevant to its role, such as DCGM and EFA exporters on GPU nodes and Slurm cluster metrics on the controller. Schema errors are rejected before rollout, while node-specific conflicts appear in extension health.

After the install, the extension appears on the cluster’s Extensions tab with its version, status, and ARN. The screenshot shows the tab for a cluster that has both the observability and user management extensions installed, and both are Active.

Figure 8: The Extensions tab for a cluster with both the observability and user management extensions installed.

According to recent reports, whichever metric store you choose, you can add an Amazon Managed Grafana workspace to the installation, so the team doesn’t need to build dashboards from scratch. After signing in to Grafana, they find two pre-created dashboards, Clusters and Jobs, as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 9: The Clusters and Jobs dashboards that come with the observability extension in Amazon Managed Grafana.

Sources indicate that the Clusters dashboard gives a single view of your HyperPod Slurm clusters, built on the metrics that the extension collects and sends to your chosen metric store. At the top, it summarizes cluster health: instance count and health, GPU and GPU memory totals, vCPUs, memory, and Amazon FSx for Lustre capacity. It also indicates the state of Slurm itself, including node states (idle, allocated, mixed, down, and draining), job queues, failed or preempted jobs, and scheduler activity. From there, you can filter by cluster, node, or GPU to drill into EFA networking, GPU performance and errors, and host-level CPU, memory, disk, and network metrics, as shown in the following screenshots. That lets you go from “is my cluster healthy?” to the root cause of an concern without leaving the dashboard.

Figure 10: The Clusters dashboard, from cluster-wide health and Slurm state down to per-node GPU, EFA, and host metrics.

According to recent reports, the Jobs dashboard moves from cluster-level health down to individual Slurm jobs. It ties each job’s resource to use back to the job itself, using metrics from the Slurm job exporter in either metric store. You can filter by cluster, job ID, job name, partition, user, or account, and see CPU, memory, GPU utilization, GPU memory, and disk I/O for each job, plus accelerator and NCCL metrics. That makes it easier to spot underused GPUs, stuck jobs, or communication bottlenecks in distributed training, as in the following screenshot.

Figure 11: The Jobs dashboard, showing resource use for individual Slurm jobs.

Later, a research team that is tuning multi-node training asks for more detail, so the administrator sends only the settings to change:.

HyperPod merges these settings into the stored configuration and applies them to every node, restarting only the components whose settings changed. When the investigation is over, setting both to null returns them to their defaults, and at no point are nodes replaced or scripts rerun.

One morning the extension indicates as Degraded. A upcoming instance group has an execution role that lacks aps:RemoteWrite, and describe-cluster-extension shows the effect:.

Once the administrator adds the permission, the nodes report healthy and the extension returns to Active, with nothing to reinstall.

According to recent reports, the user management extension manages the Linux customers and groups on every node, and who can sign in and use sudo on each node type. You declare who should exist and what they can do, and HyperPod applies it to every node, including nodes added later or replaced, so no one connects to nodes or runs scripts to add or remove a user. Users come from local accounts that you list in the configuration, from Active Directory over LDAPS, or from both, and each group names the node types (controller, login, or compute) where its members can sign in over SSH and where they get passwordless sudo.

For the platform team, security wants corporate identities, with sudo reserved for administrators, and a partner lab that isn’t in the directory needs accounts of its own. The administrator declares both sources in one configuration, with group rules that say which node types each group can sign in to and use sudo on:.

Access is explicit, so after the extension is installed only the groups that grant SSH access, along with the default ubuntu user, can sign in. Directory users keep their identities and group membership in Active Directory, while the partner lab’s users get the same IDs, home directories, and the default Slurm root account.

According to recent reports, the same configuration can be managed from the console. Choosing Manage users on the user management extension opens the cluster’s Users tab, where the administrator can add, edit, and remove groups and users, and set which node types each group can sign in to and use sudo on, as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 12: Managing groups and owners for the user management extension on the console.

When AWS publishes a new version of an extension, the administrator lists the versions that can be installed and upgrades in place without AMI updates:.

It has been revealed that hyperPod checks the stored settings against the new version’s schema and rejects the request, changing nothing, if they aren’t valid for it. Otherwise, the new version rolls out to every node, and nodes that join later get it too. Upgrades only go forward, so the administrator picks a maintenance window. Any new settings or capabilities that come with the version can then be turned on with an update like the earlier one.

Industry observers note that before the end-of-quarter run, the administrator starts an on-demand deep health check on the GPU group and then adds nodes with batch-add-cluster-nodes. The request returns as soon as HyperPod accepts it, so the administrator follows it as a cluster operation:.

As capacity arrives, each node is health checked, joins Slurm, takes its place in the topology, and gets both extensions with the same version and settings as every other node. If a GPU fails during the run, the replacement is configured and picks up the extensions the same way.

At the end of the quarter, security asks who has sudo on the controller, and the administrator answers from the API without signing in to a node:.

The answer is cluster-admins and ClusterAdmin@example.com, and the directory group’s membership is audited in the directory. Because each extension has its own ARN, the platform team’s role can update only sagemaker-user-management and the monitoring team’s role only sagemaker-observability, while security has read-only access to both. None of these permissions belongs on the cluster’s execution role. When an extension is Active, ActiveCount equals TotalCount, and Health is empty, every node runs exactly that configuration.

Sources indicate that cluster extensions, including the observability and user management extensions, have been available since November 2026 in all the regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is supported, and the other improvements in this post were unveiled earlier in 2026, with each announcement listing its Regions. There’s no additional charge for cluster extensions. You pay for the AWS resources that you use with them, such as Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, and AWS Secrets Manager.

Figure 13: The two extensions that have been available since November 2026.

A cluster is easier to run when more of it is declared, validated, converged, and observable. This year’s improvements brought that to a HyperPod Slurm cluster’s definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health, and cluster extensions, available since November 2026, bring it to the software on the nodes, the layer that changes most often. Lifecycle scripts and custom AMIs stay focused on what’s specific to your organization, and the controller node stays yours.

According to recent reports, to create a cluster as described in this post, see Getting started with SageMaker HyperPod using the AWS CLI. To get started with cluster extensions, see Cluster Extensions in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Share your feedback in the comments or through your AWS account team.

This feature has contributions across several teams. Some of the people involved in developing this include Hengyu Lou, Aman Pratap Singh, Karthick Ravi, Shubh Nisar, Nitish Sai Kommasai, Uday Singamala, Min Badar, Devanshi Desai, Yahya Hassan, Connie Chen, Kashish Tayal, Oleg Talalov, Takuma Yoshitami, Kiran Penta, Dhawal Parkar, Pradeep Cruz.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, purpose CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution. Actions to take CISA urges organizations to take the following actions: Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories. Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems. If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access. Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions. Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes. Resources CISA urges network defenders to review the following resource and apply necessary updates: Vendor Guidance Oracle’s Security Advisory: Critical Security Patch Patch – November 2026 Disclaimer The information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only.
